newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan lull expected, but peace not in sight.
newsitem.headline: Afghan lull expected, but peace not in sight.

text.p: A lull is likely to follow the Taleban Islamic movement's latest stunning victories in Afghanistan, but no end to the conflict is in sight, strategic and political analysts in neighbouring Pakistan said on Sunday.

They agreed Pakistan is in the best position among Afghanistan's neighbours to exercise a moderating influence on Taleban, whose adherents have given some controversial demonstrations of their Islamic zeal after taking Kabul.
A question mark also hangs over the Taleban's ability to rule the country's complex ethnic and tribal mix.
The Taleban forces, who now control more than half of Afghanistan and captured Kabul on Friday, have halted at Bagram airbase, 50 km (31 miles) to the north.

Beyond that, the forces of ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani have taken up up positions in an apparent move to put up tough resistance in contrast to the easy walkover they gave to a Taleban sweep in eastern Afghanistan this month climaxing with the fall of Kabul.
A hot pursuit of pro-Rabbani forces further north or going after the powerful northern warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum could prove risky.

"If they go for hot pursuit to force them to submission, they could meet mishaps just as it happened with Rabbani," Murtaza Pooya, chairman of the state-funded Institute of Strategic Studies, told Reuters in an interview on Sunday.
He was referring to the ousted president's failure to make a politial adjustment with opposition factions. "So let us hope the Taleban don't repeat what Rabbani had done."

The Taleban has ruled out a role in their government for Rabbani, his prime minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar and top military commander Ahmad Shah Masood, but has voiced the desire to settle matters with Dostum through talks.
Pooya said he expected the Taleban would try to solidate their position and reach an understanding with other factions rather than pursue the war to a military victory.

But most analysts think the pro-Rabbani forces, particularly those commanded by legendary former guerrilla commander Masood, would not give up and would mount a limited guerrilla campaign from Masood's Panjsher Valley bastion as he did against the Soviet occupation forces in 1980s.
"As far as military victories go, in the past 15 years, we have seen the pendulum swinging from one group to the other," Pooya said.
"At one time Najibullah was so strong but he went down. Rabbani also felt very strong but he collapsed. So it is very difficult to take a position," he said.

"I think there will be no major eruption in the short term," he said. "If they (Taleban) manage to keep Kabul for October and November, they will enter into the winter interlude and that will help stabilise their position."
Rabbani also seemed to have hoped that if he could hold off the Taleban assaults against Kabul for October-November, he would stabilise the situation over the winter.

"The most important question now is whether Taleban can be a unifying factor in this war between armed political groups," Pooya said. "A lot is going to depend on the statesmanship and political maturity that they demonstrate."

Taleban's execution of former president Najibullah, his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai and two other aides, and the movement's restrictions on women working in offices and girls going to schools have sent shockwaves across the world.
Special U.N. envoy Norbert Holl said he expected a "contructive solution" after he met a Taleban ruling council in Kabul on Sunday and raised the question of human rights.

Pooya said Pakistan had "a certain level of interaction" with the Taleban that was absent in the case of Rabbani, whose government accused Islamabad of helping the Taleban campaign against his government.
Pakistan denies the charge, saying it has no favourites among the Afghan factions, most of which it helped during their guerrilla war against the Soviet occupation.
"The Taleban would respect Pakistan's moderating and mediating influence with regard to their dealings with other groups and countries," Pooya said.

Pakistan was the first country to signal recognition of the Taleban administration. A delegation from Islamabad's Foreign Ministry was in Kabul on Sunday for talks on the latest situation which an official statement said were meant "to strengthen the existing brotherly relations between the two countries".
"A lot is to depend on Iran and Pakistan and how they will coordinate their moves," Pooya said.
"Viewed in the backdrop of complex tussle for power, it seems the fate of the country still hangs in the balance," the Peshawar-based nerwspaper The Frontier Post said.
"Even if they show the spirit of accommodation by luring some other stray groups to their sides, it does not ensure a lasting peace."

But Pooya said: "If the Taleban victory does not degenerate into revenge and it demonstrates a desire for healing, the entire scenario for the first time after 15 years period will assume an optimistic picture."
